title: Usability Tests vs. Concept Tests
intro: The most important distinction in UX research: **what users do** vs. **what users say**. Most teams misuse concept tests as a cheaper substitute for usability testing. This article draws the line.

learn.title: Two fundamentally different methods
learn.text:
A **usability test** gives users a realistic task on a working interface and observes what they actually do — errors, confusion, hesitation, workarounds.

A **concept test** shows users a concept or prototype and asks for reactions, preferences, or opinions.

They answer different questions. They are not interchangeable.

Usability testing evaluates 5 specific qualities (Nielsen): **learnability**, **efficiency**, **memorability**, **error recovery**, and **satisfaction**. If your test doesn't measure at least one of these, it's not a usability test.

try.q: Your team has a working checkout flow redesign. You want to know if users can complete a purchase. Which method?
try.explain: You have a working interface and want to observe behavior — that's a usability test.

learn.title: The self-report gap
learn.text:
What users **say** they want and what they actually **do** diverge constantly. Behavioral science has documented this gap for decades.

"I always read error messages carefully" → usability testing routinely shows they don't.

"I prefer fewer features" → behavioral data shows they use more features than they think.

When self-report and behavior conflict, **behavioral data wins. Every time.**

try.q: Users in a concept test say they love the new onboarding. What should you conclude?
options: They like the concept — but you don't know if they can actually use it
The onboarding is good — ship it
Users always know what works for them
Concept tests are more reliable than usability tests
try.explain: Concept tests capture opinion, not behavior. You still need usability testing to know if it actually works.

learn.title: When to use each
learn.text:
**Use usability testing when:**
→ Evaluating an existing product
→ Validating a redesign
→ Identifying friction in a critical workflow
→ Understanding failure modes

**Use concept testing when:**
→ Early-stage exploration (no interface exists yet)
→ Testing distinctly different strategic directions
→ Gathering initial reactions before committing resources

Moderated usability testing should almost always be your **default**.

try.q: You're exploring 3 radically different product directions and have no prototype yet. Which method?
try.explain: Early-stage exploration with no working interface = concept test territory.

test.q: What is the fundamental difference between usability and concept tests?
options: Usability observes behavior; concept tests collect opinions
Usability tests are faster; concept tests are slower
test.explain: Usability = what users DO. Concept = what users SAY. Different questions entirely.

test.q: When self-reported data and behavioral data conflict, which wins?
test.explain: Behavioral data wins. Always. People are consistently unreliable narrators of their own behavior.

test.q: A PM says: "We concept-tested this and users loved it, so we're skipping usability testing." What's wrong with this?
options: Concept tests can't tell you if users can actually use the interface
They should have used surveys instead
Concept tests are only for mobile apps
test.explain: Concept tests capture preference, not performance. Users saying they like something doesn't mean they can use it.

test.q: What should be your default research method when you have access to users?
test.explain: Moderated usability testing — born from behavioral science — should almost always be the default.

test.q: Which scenario is appropriate for a concept test?
options: Exploring 3 strategic directions before any design work
Identifying why users abandon a form
test.explain: Concept tests are for early-stage exploration when no working interface exists yet.
